_readme: Card fields: max ~25 words each. Facts only from CLAUDE.md 'Facts' or the linked NASA page. Unknown = TODO_VERIFY. coordsVerified=false means lat/lon still need a teammate check.

machines.name: Viking 1 Lander
machines.why: To photograph Mars up close and test its soil for signs of life.
machines.howItWorked: A small robot arm scooped soil into onboard labs that looked for signs of living things.
machines.found: The first US pictures from the surface of Mars. Its life tests were not taken as proof of life.
machines.status: Mission ended in November 1982. The lander is still at Chryse Planitia.
log: Chryse Planitia. I touched down on July 20, 1976.
I took the first US pictures from the ground on Mars.
My arm scooped red soil into my little labs. Was anything alive in it?
I worked until November 1982.
machines.numanNote: The Numans call this one 'the first to knock on the door.'
machines.teaser: This lander searched the soil for life.

hotspots.label: Scooped soil for the biology labs. TODO_VERIFY position
Took the first US photos from the Martian surface. TODO_VERIFY position

machines.name: Opportunity rover
machines.why: To look for rocks and soil that show whether Mars once had water.
machines.howItWorked: Six wheels, solar panels for power, and a robot arm with tools to study rocks up close.
machines.found: Evidence that Mars was once wet, including small round hematite grains called 'blueberries'.
machines.status: Last heard from June 10, 2018, during a dust storm. Mission declared over in February 2019.
log: Meridiani Planum. They planned for 90 days.
I drove about 28 miles over almost 15 years.
I found signs that Mars was once wet.
In 2018 a dust storm covered the Sun, and I never woke up.
machines.numanNote: The Numans say dust storms still sing its name.
machines.teaser: Built for 90 days. Lasted almost 15 years.

hotspots.label: Turned sunlight into power. Dust storms blocked it. TODO_VERIFY position
Held tools to study rocks up close. TODO_VERIFY position
Six wheels carried it about 28 miles. TODO_VERIFY position

machines.name: InSight lander
machines.why: To study the deep inside of Mars.
machines.howItWorked: A seismometer sat on the ground under a dome that blocked wind and heat, listening for shaking.
machines.found: More than 1,300 marsquakes. The biggest was about magnitude 5 in May 2022.
machines.status: Dust covered its solar panels. NASA ended the mission in December 2022.
log: Elysium Planitia. I landed in November 2018.
I set my seismometer on the ground under a dome. Then I listened.
Mars rumbled more than 1,300 times.
Dust slowly covered my solar panels, and in December 2022 I went quiet.
machines.numanNote: The Numans tune their songs to the rhythm of marsquakes.

hotspots.label: Covered the seismometer to block wind and heat. TODO_VERIFY position
Round panels made power until dust covered them. TODO_VERIFY position
Placed instruments on the ground. TODO_VERIFY position

machines.name: Ingenuity helicopter
machines.why: To test whether a helicopter could fly in the thin air of Mars.
machines.howItWorked: Two rotors spin in opposite directions, very fast, to grip the thin Martian air.
machines.found: The first powered, controlled flight on another planet, on April 19, 2021. It flew 72 times.
machines.status: Rotor damage ended its mission in January 2024. It still rests in Jezero Crater.
log: Jezero Crater. I rode to Mars under Perseverance.
On April 19, 2021, I lifted off. No one had flown on another planet before.
I flew 72 times.
I carry a tiny piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer.
machines.numanNote: The Numans had never seen a machine dance in the air before.
machines.teaser: The first aircraft to fly on another planet.

hotspots.label: Two rotors spun opposite ways to grip thin air. TODO_VERIFY position
Charged its batteries between flights. TODO_VERIFY position

machines.name: Apollo 11 descent stage
machines.why: To land the first astronauts on the Moon and bring them home safely.
machines.howItWorked: The lower half of the lander Eagle. When it was time to leave, the top half fired its engine and lifted off from it.
machines.found: Astronauts set up a laser reflector, a quake sensor and a solar wind experiment here.
machines.status: Still at Tranquility Base, with the plaque attached to it.
log: Sea of Tranquility. I landed here on July 20, 1969.
Two astronauts stepped down my ladder and walked on the Moon.
When it was time to go, the top half of me fired its engine and left.
I stayed behind, with a plaque on my leg.
machines.teaser: It was a launch pad for the trip home.

machines.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle
machines.why: To let astronauts drive farther and explore more of the Moon.
machines.howItWorked: A battery-powered car. Two astronauts sat side by side and drove it across the dusty valley.
machines.found: It carried the crew around Taurus-Littrow, the last Apollo landing site.
log: Taurus-Littrow. I arrived in December 1972, folded up on the side of a lander.
I ran on batteries and drove 30.5 kilometers in all.
I was the last Apollo rover. I am still parked in the valley.
machines.numanNote: The Numans like that it has wheels. They do not.
machines.teaser: A car that drove on the Moon.

machines.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
machines.why: To map the Moon and find good, safe places for future explorers.
machines.howItWorked: A laser called LOLA measures how high or low the ground is, building a 3D map.
machines.found: It mapped the Moon's surface, temperature and radiation, and helps find water near the South Pole.
machines.status: Still working. The longest-lived Moon orbiter ever.
log: Launched June 18, 2009. I have circled the Moon ever since.
I measure every hill and crater with a laser.
I look for water ice near the South Pole for future explorers.
machines.numanNote: The Numans say LRO knows the Moon better than the Moon does.
machines.teaser: It maps the whole Moon from orbit.

machines.name: Blue Ghost Mission 1 lander
machines.why: To deliver 10 NASA science payloads to the Moon.
machines.howItWorked: Its Electrodynamic Dust Shield used electric fields to push dust off surfaces.
machines.found: It tested how lunar dust sticks to materials and ways to keep dust off.
log: Mare Crisium. I carried 10 NASA experiments to the Moon.
One used electricity to push sticky Moon dust off a camera and a panel.
Moon dust gets into everything. Now we know more about stopping it.
machines.numanNote: The Numans named it 'the dust whisperer.'
machines.teaser: It tested ways to clear dust off surfaces.
machines.todo: Landing date and end of mission not shown on the linked NASA page; arrived year 2025 from the team outline.

machines.name: Voyager 1
machines.why: To fly by Jupiter and Saturn, then keep going.
machines.howItWorked: A big dish antenna points home to send data across billions of miles.
machines.found: It became the first human-made object in interstellar space, in August 2012.
machines.status: Still sending data. More than 16 billion miles away, nearing one light-day from Earth.
log: I launched in 1977 and flew past Jupiter and Saturn.
In August 2012 I left the Sun's bubble and entered interstellar space.
Engineers turn my instruments off one by one to save power.
I am still talking to Earth.
machines.numanNote: The Numans can hear it humming far away.
machines.teaser: Its signal takes almost a day to reach Earth.

machines.name: Voyager 2
machines.why: To study the giant outer planets up close.
machines.howItWorked: It used each planet's gravity to swing on to the next one.
machines.found: The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune. It found new moons and rings at both.
machines.status: In interstellar space since 2018, still sending data.
log: I launched on August 20, 1977.
I am the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.
At Neptune I found five moons, four rings and a Great Dark Spot.
In 2018 I joined my twin in interstellar space.
machines.numanNote: The Numans think Voyager 2 is the braver twin. Do not tell Voyager 1.
machines.teaser: The only visitor to Uranus and Neptune.

machines.name: New Horizons
machines.why: To study Pluto, its moons and other icy worlds in the Kuiper Belt.
machines.howItWorked: A nuclear power source (an RTG, a spare from Cassini) made about 250 watts at launch.
machines.found: The first close look at Pluto (2015) and at Arrokoth (2019), the most distant object ever explored up close.
machines.status: Still flying outward through the Kuiper Belt.
log: I launched on January 19, 2006.
On July 14, 2015, I flew past Pluto and its moons.
In 2019 I reached Arrokoth, the farthest world ever explored up close.
I am still heading out into the dark.
machines.numanNote: The Numans say it took the long way and enjoyed it.
machines.teaser: It hibernates to save power on long trips.

machines.name: Cassini
machines.why: To study Saturn, its rings and its moons in great detail.
machines.howItWorked: It was the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, circling it for 13 years.
machines.found: Water ice and vapor spraying from the moon Enceladus.
machines.status: Mission ended September 2017. It was steered into Saturn on purpose.
log: I launched in 1997 and began orbiting Saturn in 2004.
I saw ice spraying from the moon Enceladus.
When my fuel ran low, I dove into Saturn on purpose.
That kept Enceladus and Titan clean for future explorers.
machines.numanNote: The Numans call this 'the kindest ending.'
machines.teaser: Its ending was planned to protect Saturn's moons.
